name: Rosa Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crew fitting floor joists and exterior doors on building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and plenty of practice correcting a doorway that looked square on paper, though I still work with the crew rather than sit in an office. My husband Daniel and I have two children in school, a mortgage, ordinary pay for this trade and about three months of expenses saved. Some other contractors work nearby, but I have never used an AI tool and do not chase a new one for the sake of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that the office may print a better list, but the door still has to swing in the actual opening. The square and level remain in my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small software change would leave my work and pay mostly alone. Three months saved gives us some room, though a mortgage and school costs mean I cannot be careless with a paid day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current joist and door work and check the opening before signing the materials list. In the first year I would return any new list that leaves out a measured door width.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. I would rather spend the saved paperwork time teaching a young carpenter to hang a door straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which width gets left out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An old doorway can be wider at the floor than at the top. I would mark both numbers on the timber before anyone cuts a new frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let the apprentice use AI for a list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentice can try it after learning to measure the wall. I would not sign a cut list just because a screen says the numbers match.

say: **Old door openings** need two real measurements before a carpenter cuts a new frame.
**Better lists** cannot replace a square and level.
think: My **work and pay** stay broadly safe in the plateau.
Our **three-month reserve** gives room while school and mortgage costs continue.
do: **Keep** fitting floor joists and exterior doors while checking every opening at the building site.
**Return** lists that omit actual door width.
feel: **Calm** about income, still careful with paid site time.
S0.quote: An old doorway can be wider at the floor than at the top.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and first teaches the younger carpenter to measure an actual doorway.
Her **moderate savings** support calm while ordinary household bills remain important.

steps.text: Keep joist and door work with site measurements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say office buying and booking can change first, but a robot will not be fitting every door at once. A new schedule needs the time for measuring an old opening, not only hanging the finished door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the planner assumes a standard opening, the boss could cut our paid hours for each job. With three months saved, several short pay slips would trouble the mortgage, even though a few other contractors are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a written log of seven door jobs, separating measuring, cutting and fitting time. In the first year I would take the log to the site manager and postpone our planned garden work if paid hours actually fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even if I sound matter of fact. I know exactly which mortgage bill arrives before the next building site pays us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the manager see in the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One old doorway needed the frame cut twice because the wall narrowed near the ceiling. I would put the extra hour beside the plan, not hide it in a daily total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change contractors now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not for a plan that has not been used. If a posted nearby door-fitting job offered steadier hours and pay that covered our bills, I would apply after seeing my hours shrink.

say: **Office schedules** change before capable robots can fit physical doors on building sites.
**Old openings** need measured time in job plans.
think: Shorter **paid hours** could reduce my own income.
Three months saved and **some nearby work** may not cover repeated short payslips.
do: **Log** seven door jobs with measuring and fitting times.
**Postpone** garden work if paid hours fall.
**Apply** for nearby posted fitting if hours shrink and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about income despite a composed voice.
S1.quote: I know exactly which mortgage bill arrives before the next building site pays us.
fieldNote: She ties **schedule errors** to a plausible cut in her own paid hours.
Her **job application** waits for reduced hours and a posted nearby role with bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Postpone garden work if site hours fall
Apply for nearby posted door fitting if hours shrink and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can handle plans and buying, while capable hands-on robots arrive about 2031. There are three years of real door and joist work between those dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose shifts after 2031 if a robot fits doors and lays joists quickly. Our three-month reserve and a few nearby contractors give me a way to search, but the mortgage will not wait for a long one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put part of each full pay week into savings while the bills allow, starting now. After 2028 I would ask two nearby contractors about posted repair work and apply if robots cut my shifts after 2031, but only for a job with hours and wages that cover our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the future pay, with a plan I can start this week. I will not spend the children’s cushion buying a certificate for a job nobody has advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you save from a full week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel and I could set aside thirty if groceries and the mortgage are paid first. A short week would mean no extra saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for robot work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a contractor offered paid time, safe hands-on instruction and a posted local job at enough wage. I would not enrol on a course advertised without an opening.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches plans before capable door-fitting robots around 2031.
**Physical carpentry** remains during the three-year gap.
think: Robots could cut **joist and door shifts** after 2031.
A **three-month reserve** cannot carry a long search with the mortgage due.
do: **Save** thirty from each full pay week after mortgage and groceries.
**Apply** for posted nearby repair if robots cut shifts and pay and hours cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about future wages, with a small saving plan.
S2.quote: I will not spend the children’s cushion buying a certificate for a job nobody has advertised.
fieldNote: She plans **new savings** from full paid weeks rather than moving current reserves.
Her **training interest** remains conditional and is not tagged as actual retraining.

steps.text: Save thirty from full paid weeks after mortgage and groceries
Apply for posted nearby repair if robots cut shifts and pay and hours cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to see a machine work on a crooked doorway before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Capable field robots follow around 2034, and I would want the failed fittings counted as well as the good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be near fifty then, with children getting older and the mortgage perhaps still due. I might learn site inspection if someone shows me the work, but a certificate alone would not put food on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading door fitting and visit a robot trial with the site manager. If a posted nearby inspection job has safe duties, paid hands-on training and wages covering our bills, I would take the course before 2031 and apply after 2031; otherwise I would keep the crew work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but five years allows me to see the machine before changing trade. I will not give up paid hours for an untested offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trial failure should be recorded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot might hang a door that catches on an uneven floor. I would record the gap, the correction and who checked the final swing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if inspection pays less than your current wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel and I would compare the new pay with mortgage, food and school costs. I could accept a little less only if those bills stayed covered without using savings each month.

say: **Crooked-door trials** should come before capable robots can fit building-site doors around 2034.
**Failures** must be logged alongside good fits.
think: A **site inspection** move could work if paid hands-on teaching is tied to real local work.
The **mortgage and children** require steady bill-covering pay.
do: **Visit** a robot door-fitting trial with the manager.
**Take** paid inspection course only for posted nearby safe bill-covering job.
**Apply** after 2031 if trained and safe duties and wages hold.
feel: **Anxious** about wages, with time to inspect the option.
S3.quote: A robot might hang a door that catches on an uneven floor.
fieldNote: Her **trial** checks a visible floor gap and records the human correction.
Her **course and application** require posted nearby work, paid instruction, safe duties and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Observe door-fitting robot trial before deciding
Take paid inspection course for posted nearby safe bill-covering job
Apply after 2031 for posted nearby inspection if trained, safe and bill-covering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable site robots around 2039. I would use the years to keep the mortgage shrinking and teach apprentices how a door feels when it hangs correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my fifties when robots can do the physical work. Ten years gives us time, but if the site trims good door-fitting hours then, I will still need another wage with the children starting their own lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew and pay an extra twenty toward the mortgage from each full cheque after ordinary bills. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for posted local building-maintenance work only if the wage and hours cover our bills and any required training is paid and safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later earnings, not frozen by the long horizon. The family can make small steady payments while I keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fitted door can tell an apprentice more through one swing than a perfect building-site drawing. A level and square would come next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the extra twenty is not there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would skip the extra twenty on a short pay week. The three-month reserve is for a lost week, not for making an extra mortgage payment.

say: **2036 thinking AI** arrives before capable site robots can fit physical doors around 2039.
think: Fewer **door-fitting hours** could still hurt household income during my later working years.
Ten years allows **debt payments** from full wages.
do: **Keep** leading door fitting on current sites.
**Pay** twenty extra on mortgage from full cheques after bills.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted local maintenance only with bill-covering hours, wage and paid safe training.
feel: **Anxious** about later income, with time to reduce debt.
S4.quote: A fitted door can tell an apprentice more through one swing than a perfect building-site drawing.
fieldNote: Her **extra debt payment** comes from future full wages, not the existing reserve.
Her **later application** keeps posted local work, wage, hours, paid training and safety as conditions.

steps.text: Keep leading door fitting on current building sites
Pay twenty extra on mortgage from full cheques after bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because door-fitting robots around 2031 might cut the paid hours that cover our mortgage and school bills. A posted nearby repair role with reliable hours and pay would help, as would paid training tied to a safe inspection job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a robot-fitted door feels right after the photograph is taken. I want a carpenter to swing the robot-fitted door before the family moves in.

portrait: **Rosa Jensen**, 43, leads a door and floor-joist crew with a vocational trade certificate.
She and husband Daniel have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, ordinary trade pay and about three months saved.
She has **never used AI** and prefers the square, level and physical swing of a door to screen results.
In **Steady Disruption**, she logs seven jobs and may seek posted nearby fitting work if paid hours shrink.
The **2028 picture** worries her most because robot fitting could reduce shifts before the mortgage is safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut door and joist shifts after 2031 while household bills continue.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **nearby repair job** with reliable hours and bill-covering wages would protect income.
Paid **inspection training** attached to a safe posted role would create a second option.
headlineQuote: I want a carpenter to swing the robot-fitted door before the family moves in.
